items.title: Climate change and displacement - How people are being forced to flee their homes | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Over the past 10 years, climate change has displaced an average of 70,000 people, every day. This, according to figures from the UN Refugee Agency, UNHCR. Poorer countries are particularly hard hit.

There is no universal legal framework that would offer these people protection. Climate-induced displacement is not recognised as a valid ground for asylum under the Geneva Convention.  Now, three countries in Latin America, the Pacific and Asia are responding to an emergency that directly affects each of them. 

One of these countries is Bangladesh. It is one of the places most severely affected by climate change. In 2024, around 2.4 million people in Bangladesh became internally displaced. Most of them lost their homes due to a natural disaster. Cyclones and tropical storms cause devastating damage, while rising sea levels are flooding mangrove forests and agricultural land. Melting glaciers in the Himalayas are causing flooding along the rivers. In new model villages, communities displaced by soil erosion and salinization are being provided with accommodation and land.

In Colombia, pressure from lawyers led to the legal recognition of the first victims of climate change. The historic ruling recognizes that displacement is not only caused by violence and armed conflict, but also by environmental factors.

In the Pacific, regional solidarity is being prioritized in the face of rising sea levels, which threaten the very existence of several nations. At the same time, policy is shaped by a recognition of the deep ties people have to their homeland and their history. For people here, leaving would be tantamount to exile.

items.title: What we can learn from the tragedy of Jason Arday
items.author: Vox
items.content:
<article>In 2023, Jason Arday was appointed a professor of sociology at Cambridge University, making him the youngest Black professor there. Shortly after that, allegations that Arday plagiarized parts of his Ph.D thesis began. 

Those allegations quickly spiraled into questions about every aspect of his life. After relentless attacks online and in the media, Arday resigned from this position, and a few days later he was found dead, likely taking his own life.

Tyler Austin Harper, a staff writer for The Atlantic, spoke to Vox about who is to blame for this tragedy. Is it the institutions that put Arday on a pedestal? Or the racist attacks and accusations of DEI online?

items.title: WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange: Idol and public enemy no. 1 | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>For some he's a hero. For others, he’s public enemy number one. Certainly, his revelations challenged US power. This film follows the WikiLeaks founder’s extraordinary life story.

With the publication of thousands of secret US military and diplomatic documents in 2010, WikiLeaks ushered in a new information age. Suddenly, thanks to founder Julian Assange, state secrets were out in the open — and under scrutiny.

For many journalists and activists, Assange was a pioneer who used new technologies to evade both censorship and reprisals. For others, he symbolized an openness that could bring both nation states and multinational corporations to their knees.

For seven years, Assange sought refuge in the Ecuadorian embassy in London. After that, he spent five years in a British high-security prison facing US charges of espionage carrying a potential sentence of 175 years. Following a deal with the US Department of Justice, he was finally released in the summer of 2024.

The film tells the story of Julian Assange and asks the question: in a world of radical change, what remains of the fight for truth?

items.title: Why nonalcoholic wine is so expensive
items.author: Vox
items.content:
<article>08/20/26 correction: the voiceover @ 4:58 should say "decreasing pressure to lower the boiling point of alcohol" rather than "increasing pressure to lower the boiling point of alcohol"

The non-alcoholic beverage industry has exploded from once-a-year “Dry January” experiments to one of the fastest-growing categories in food and beverage, largely driven by younger consumers who are drinking less but still wanting the rituals and community of socializing. US sales of non-alcoholic beer, wine, and spirits have grown over 20 percent year over year, and analysts project that the no-alcohol market will grow by over $4 billion by 2028.

With the wine world experiencing one of its biggest downturns in decades, small businesses and food scientists are turning to non-alcoholic wines as a potential alternative. Some are using technology and chemistry to produce premium dealcoholized wines, while others, like Burden of Proof in Los Angeles, are recreating the community feel of wine shops through NA-only storefronts.

However, even as consumers turn away from alcohol, many are still shocked by the sticker price of alcohol-free wine. How could something with alcohol removed cost just as much as something with alcohol? The answer is a mix of the high cost of dealcoholizing technology and the price attached to a growing movement.

Read more about the non-alcoholic beverage trend:

items.title: Mission in the Alps: The mountain rescuers | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>The picturesque Bavarian Alps, beloved by mountaineers and hiking enthusiasts. But overconfidence or sudden weather changes can create emergencies. Then, mountain rescuers are the last hope.

On the Blaueis ("blue ice") Glacier, a young mountaineer is in distress. Alone when a thick fog rolls in, he's unable to continue. A team from the Ramsau Mountain Rescue Service sets out immediately, but the fog becomes a problem for them as well. The mountain rescuers' keen sense of direction is put to the test: Two teams search from different directions for the man, who is likely already severely hypothermic.

A hiker has fallen 40 meters in the Bavarian Alps. The air rescue team prepares to fly to the accident site using a helicopter. There's no information yet on the condition of the victim. But experience dictates that in a fall from this height, the rescuers should prepare for the worst.

Both missions end well. But that is not always the case. The memory of Peter Hildebrandt, former head of operations in Ramsau, is ever-present. He fell to his death during a mission. The mountain rescuers are always aware that they, too, are risking their lives.

items.title: Modern Computer Architecture & Organization • Jim Ledin & Maciej «MJ» Jedrzejewski • GOTO 2026
items.author: GOTO Conferences
items.content:
<article>This interview was recorded for the GOTO Book Club. #GOTOcon #GOTObookclub
http://gotopia.tech/bookclub

Check out more here:
https://gotopia.tech/articles/452

Jim Ledin - President at Ledin Engineering & Author of “Modern Computer Architecture and Organization” @jledin1 
Maciej «MJ» Jedrzejewski - Tech Agnostic Architect & Author of “Master Software Architecture” @learnsoftwarearchitecture 

RESOURCES
Jim
https://www.linkedin.com/in/jimledin
https://x.com/ledin_eng
https://github.com/jledin
https://ledin.com

MJ
https://github.com/meaboutsoftware
https://www.linkedin.com/in/jedrzejewski-maciej
https://www.fractionalarchitect.io

Links
https://youtu.be/wNT2qkusVrA
https://youtu.be/Pv0cfsastFs
https://youtu.be/cI9dfQLTXlU
https://youtu.be/a2DvXnecXVk

DESCRIPTION
Jim Ledin — author of Modern Computer Architecture and Organization, now in its third edition — joins Maciej "MJ" Jedrzejewski to talk through the book's two brand-new chapters on GPUs and large language models, and the specific challenge of writing about hardware that changes faster than a book can ship. Ledin's approach was to focus on durable architectural principles (parallelism, memory bandwidth, tensor processing, and how systems scale from one chip to an entire data center rack) rather than chasing the current state of the art. For the LLM chapter specifically, he chose GPT-2 as the teaching example precisely because it's open-source and small enough to trace by hand — and because, as he explains, the transformer architecture underneath today's frontier models is fundamentally the same structure, just scaled up.

The most concrete takeaway for engineers: the AI buildout's real bottleneck right now isn't compute, it's memory bandwidth — a shift driving high-bandwidth memory production at the expense of consumer RAM, which Ledin illustrates with a blunt data point (a 32GB DDR5 stick that cost $69 a year ago now runs $440). But asked which single chapter would most change how a working developer with no hardware background thinks about their own code, Ledin doesn't point to AI at all — he points to the chapter on pipelining and cache hierarchy, arguing that most of the thousandfold speedup from 1980s PCs to today came from those optimizations, not clock speed, and that writing cache- and pipeline-friendly code is still one of the highest-leverage skills a developer can have.

The modern enterprise has evolved in many ways since some of the typical Enterprise Architecture principles and practices emerged.

In this talk, Simon Rohrer will explain how the nature of the modern enterprise means many legacy Enterprise Architecture principles and practices are no longer applicable.

He makes some suggestions on how a modern EA practice can incorporate agile, DevOps, Systems Thinking and socio-technical ways of working at scale to achieve both short term business value, as well as effecting long term technology and organisation transformation - supporting better value, sooner, safer and happier; breaking dependencies rather than managing them.

items.title: How Former VP Dick Cheney Led the Charge on the War on Terror (full documentary) | FRONTLINE (PBS)
items.author: FRONTLINE PBS | Official
items.content:
<article>An investigation into former Vice President Dick Cheney’s role as chief architect of the war on terror — and his internal war with the CIA. (Aired 2006)

This journalism is made possible by viewers like you. Donate to FRONTLINE now: https://bit.ly/47DFzCb

And support your local PBS station here: https://www.pbs.org/donate

In “The Dark Side,” which aired in 2006, FRONTLINE investigated the internal war that was waged between the intelligence community and former Vice President Dick Cheney after the attacks on Sept. 11, 2001.

Just after the attacks, Cheney told Americans: “A lot of what needs to be done here will have to be done quietly, without any discussion, using sources and methods that are available to our intelligence agencies.”. He warned the public that the government would have to operate on the “dark side.”

This documentary detailed the vice president’s role as the chief architect of the war on terror, and his battle with former Director of Central Intelligence George Tenet for control of the “dark side.” After 9/11, both leaders acted fast to prepare the U.S. for a new kind of war. But soon a debate grew over the goals of the war on terror, and the decision to go to war in Iraq. 

Drawing on more than 40 interviews and thousands of documents, this film provided a step-by-step examination of what happened inside the councils of war at that time. 

Cheney died on Nov. 3, 2025, at age 84. 

“The Dark Side” was written, produced and directed by Michael Kirk. It was produced and reported by Jim Gilmore. The executive editor of FRONTLINE was Louis Wiley, Jr. The executive producer of FRONTLINE was David Fanning. 

In the run-up to the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks, we are making a number of seminal documentaries from the days and years after 9/11 available to stream on YouTube for the first time. Starting with today’s release of “The Dark Side” and continuing every Tuesday until the week of Sept. 11, these documentaries offer a profound historical record of the attacks, what led up to them, the U.S. government's response, and the ripple effects across the U.S. and the world.

items.title: What’s Going On Inside the Sun? With Lika Guhathakurta
items.author: StarTalk
items.content:
<article>T-Mobile 5G Home Internet. https://T-Mobile.com/HomeInternet

Get the NEW StarTalk book, 'Lost in Space: 5,000 Facts for Navigating the Universe' on Amazon: https://amzn.to/4cCD19e

What does it look like beneath the surface of the sun? On this episode, Neil deGrasse Tyson and comedian Chuck Nice discuss the heliosphere, the Parker Solar Probe, and solar storms with heliophysicist Lika Guhathakurta.

How do we know what’s going on inside the sun? We break down the techniques heliophysicists use to infer activity beneath the surface. Plus, how much matter has the sun lost since it began the fusion process? Learn how the sun maintains its mass despite all the energy it radiates.

We explore the sounds the sun would make if you could hear it in space. How might that sound differ between large and small stars? Can you see the boiling plasma on the surface of the sun? We discuss the heliosphere, the region outside the sun influenced by the solar wind, and how it protects us from solar radiation. How have NASA spacecraft “punched through” the heliosphere? What was the mission of the Parker Solar Probe, and what is it doing now?

How do coronal mass ejections interact with our atmosphere? Learn about how the sun creates aurora and Neil and Lika’s experiences with solar storms. Could a coronal mass ejection wipe out all electronics on Earth—or in orbit? What would happen if we had another Carrington Event, the most intense geomagnetic storm in recorded history?

Eons: Life and Death on Pangea
Set during the Permian Period, hundreds of millions of years ago, EONS: LIFE AND DEATH ON PANGEA transports viewers to a world shaped by the supercontinent Pangea, extreme climate shifts, and ecosystems unlike anything seen today. From mega-monsoons and vast deserts to giant terrestrial animals, bizarre marine life, and massive volcanic eruptions, the series traces how Earth reached the brink of ecological collapse, and how life ultimately recovered. The “Great Dying” remains one of the most dramatic examples of how environmental change can reshape life on Earth.</article>

items.title: War in Sudan - Fleeing violence and hunger | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>For over three years, Sudan has been caught up in a devastating civil war. Both the Sudanese Armed Forces and their opponents, the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), have been accused of committing war crimes in their struggle for power.

It's the world's worst humanitarian crisis. Millions of Sudanese have been forced to flee their homes; hundreds of thousands have lost their lives. The RSF's capture of the city of El-Fasher in the Darfur region in October 2025 marked one of the bloodiest chapters in this ongoing conflict. In just a few weeks, the militias are believed to have massacred over 60-thousand residents. A few of the survivors that managed to flee tell their stories in this documentary. They recount the atrocities: rapes, murders, bombardments, hunger and the death march to the displacement camp.

Sudan's civil war would likely have ended already if both sides weren't being backed by foreign powers. The RSF has the support of the United Arab Emirates, who are thought to be providing its fighters with military assistance. Meanwhile, Egypt is supplying the Sudanese army with money and weapons, as are Iran and Russia.

In El-Obeid— a city held by Sudan's military but increasingly under attack by the RSF — fears of a repeat of the bloodshed seen in El-Fasher are rising. Those who can are boarding buses or trucks bound for the capital, Khartoum, despite having little hope of receiving international aid. Sudan is among the countries worst affected by US President Donald Trump's foreign aid cuts.

items.title: Racing to detect viruses before they reach humans | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>What if the next pandemic could be detected before it spreads? 

In the rainforests of the Central African Republic, researchers are tracking pathogens that can spread between animals and humans. By studying bats, gorillas and other wildlife, they hope to identify potential threats before they become global outbreaks. 

Viruses that originate in animals have repeatedly changed the course of human history. Ebola, COVID-19 and mpox are among the diseases caused by pathogens that jump from animals to humans. To better understand the risks, WWF veterinarian Frédéric Singa works in the Dzanga-Sangha Protected Areas, where he captures bats, collects samples from gorilla droppings, and collaborates with local communities to identify which pathogens are circulating in the forest.

The samples Singa collects are analyzed in a field laboratory before being sent abroad, including to Germany, for further testing. Professor Fabian Leendertz of the Helmholtz Institute for One Health in Greifswald studies how new infectious diseases emerge and maps global risk areas. The work highlights the close connection between human, animal and environmental health.

items.title: We Fired the Most Iconic Sniper Rifles (Over Last 100 Years)
items.author: History Hit
items.content:
<article>How has the sniper rifle evolved over the last 100 years? It's time to find out!

Luke Tomes returns to the Royal Armouries to fire some of the most iconic British sniper rifles of the last 100 years. As always, he is joined by Keeper of Firearms & Artillery, Jonathan Ferguson, who talks him through the history, design and development of each rifle, showcasing how British military sniping has evolved from the battlefields of the Second World War to the modern era.

First up is the Lee-Enfield No. 4 Mk. I (T), the dedicated sniper variant of the British Lee-Enfield rifle developed during the Second World War. Chambered in .303 British, the No. 4 Mk. I (T) was selected for its accuracy and fitted with a telescopic sight, transforming the already proven Lee-Enfield into a specialist precision weapon. Used extensively by British and Commonwealth forces, it combined the fast, smooth action of the Lee-Enfield with the precision required for long-range shooting. It established a foundation for British military sniping that would influence specialist rifles for decades to come.

Second is the L42A1, which represented the next major step in the evolution of the British military sniper rifle. Introduced in the 1970s, the L42A1 was developed from the No. 4 Lee-Enfield and converted to fire the 7.62×51mm NATO cartridge, reflecting the wider adoption of the NATO standard. Retaining the familiar Lee-Enfield action while incorporating a new calibre and improved telescopic sighting system, the L42A1 served British forces for several decades. It demonstrated how a proven wartime design could be adapted to meet the demands of the modern battlefield.

Third up is the L96A1, a rifle that marked a dramatic departure from the Lee-Enfield lineage. Developed by Accuracy International and adopted by the British Army in the 1980s, the L96A1 was chambered in 7.62×51mm NATO and built specifically as a modern precision rifle. Its distinctive design, with a rigid chassis and highly adjustable stock, prioritised accuracy, durability and consistency. The L96A1 became one of the defining British sniper rifles of the late 20th century and helped establish Accuracy International as a major name in precision rifle development.

Next is the L115A3, a long-range precision rifle introduced into British service in the 2000s. Also produced by Accuracy International, the L115A3 is chambered in .338 Lapua Magnum, giving it considerably greater effective range than the 7.62mm rifles that preceded it. Designed for extreme long-range precision, it provided British snipers with increased reach and accuracy in demanding operational environments. The rifle became particularly well known through its use in Afghanistan and represents the move towards larger-calibre systems designed to engage targets at exceptional distances.

Last but not least is the L129A1, a semi-automatic designated marksman rifle introduced to British service in response to the demands of modern combat. Chambered in 7.62×51mm NATO, it is based on the AR-10 pattern and provides accurate, rapid follow-up fire at medium and extended ranges. Unlike the bolt-action sniper rifles that preceded it, the L129A1 is designed to give infantry a precision capability while retaining the speed and versatility of a semi-automatic action. Together with the L115A3, it demonstrates how British military precision firepower has evolved to encompass different roles, from traditional long-range sniping to providing accurate fire in support of infantry operations.

items.title: Freud was more right than you think | The Gray Area
items.author: Vox
items.content:
<article>Sigmund Freud is probably the most famous psychoanalyst. Yet many of his theories have been critiqued or discredited. So is there anything we can still learn from the father of psychoanalysis?

Subscribe to our channel! http://goo.gl/0bsAjO

In today’s episode Sean speaks with professor Mark Solms, author of The Only Cure: Freud and the Neuroscience of Mental Healing. Mark argues that while Freud may have been wrong about many things, he was right about one important thing: the human mind cannot be fully understood on purely biological terms. He believes that modern psychiatry has become focused on treating mental suffering like a chemical problem, instead of focusing on emotional and psychological aspects.

Sean and Mark discuss the conscious versus the unconscious mind, whether psychoanalysis is the best therapy, and why Freud is still relevant today.

items.title: The Mölln attacks - Surviving racist terror | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>In 1992, three people died in an arson attack carried out by neo-Nazis in Mölln, northern Germany. They were relatives of İbrahim Arslan, who was seven years old at the time. The film follows the family as they come to terms with their trauma.

Ibrahim survived the fire, but lost his sister, cousin and grandmother. In the wake of the Mölln attacks, the town received thousands of letters of solidarity. They were archived - and forgotten for almost three decades.

Woven into İbrahim's moving quest to uncover the past and his encounters with three of the letter-writers, the rediscovered letters form a visual and emotional bridge between the past and the present. The film follows İbrahim and his siblings, painting a sensitive portrait of a trauma that continues to shape their lives to this day.

For İbrahim, coming to terms with the past means one thing above all else: fighting racism and championing a culture of remembrance centered on the perspectives of those affected. His brother Namik, on the other hand, is only beginning to process the trauma of their shared experiences.

The film also uncovers a powerful sense of solidarity - one that the victims and survivors were not previously aware of. The film is a plea for a new form of remembrance, one that takes the voices of survivors seriously and finally gives them the space and recognition they deserve.

items.title: The Insane US-Japan Currency Bailout
items.author: Patrick Boyle
items.content:
<article>Level up your note-taking with Plaud NotePro at https://bit.ly/4c9s3bC and use code PBOYLE for 15% off
Amazon: https://amzn.to/4xFP79Q

In July 2026, the US Treasury did something it hadn't done since 1998: it intervened in the currency markets to prop up the Japanese yen — and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, a former Soros hedge fund manager, ran the trade in the strangest way possible, selling euros instead of dollars without telling the ECB. But this was never really about Japan. It was about protecting American borrowing costs at a moment when the US is paying more to borrow than it has in decades — with 30-year Treasury yields hitting their highest since 2001. This video breaks down the US-Japan yen intervention, the carry trade, the FIMA facility, and Bessent's huge bet on falling interest rates, and asks the real question underneath it all: is the Treasury Secretary a visionary macro trader, or a cornered man making an enormous gamble with the balance sheet of the United States? A look at currency intervention, the eroding "exorbitant privilege" of the dollar, and why America's cheap borrowing may be coming to an end.

items.title: Tiny rooms at sky-high prices | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Berlin was once known for its cheap rents. Now, overpriced tiny rooms have become the norm. Many apartments are listed as furnished short-term rentals, which can cost twice as much as standard apartments. This business model is more profitable for landlords because of a gap in German rental laws. 

The "Mietpreisbremse," which regulates rent prices, doesn't apply to apartments that are legitimately rented for "temporary use." So, landlords advertise them as such, even when they don't actually meet that definition. They also charge extra fees for furniture, without having to explain or itemize those costs.

items.title: 1897: To the North Pole in a hydrogen balloon | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Three men, a hydrogen balloon, and a shared dream of reaching the North Pole. In 1897, the Andrée expedition vanished without a trace. It wasn’t until 1930 that their preserved bodies, diaries, and photographs were discovered on Kvitøya.

At the end of the 19th century, the North Pole was a blank spot on the map — a symbol of adventure, glory, and scientific progress. On July 11, 1897, Swedish nationals August Salomon Andrée, Nils Strindberg, and Knut Frænkel began their expedition to the North Pole. Starting from the Svalbard archipelago, north of Norway, the three set out in a hydrogen balloon. The whole world was watching; their homeland held its breath. After carrier pigeons delivered some optimistic messages, contact was suddenly lost. Thirty-three years of radio silence followed.

In early August 1930, following a summer of significant ice retreat, seal hunters on the island of Kvitøya, the "White Island" in the far north of the Svalbard archipelago, stumbled upon the expedition's remains. In the snow lay well-preserved bodies, as well the group's equipment: hundreds of items, including morphine and opium, intact notebooks and rolls of film, 93 of which were recovered.

What do these photographs and carefully kept diaries reveal about the expedition? How did the three men end up on this island — and how, when, and why did they die?

items.title: Inside the Fight Against SARS | Hong Kong: Chasing the Virus (full documentary) | FRONTLINE/World
items.author: FRONTLINE PBS | Official
items.content:
<article>The story of how the SARS outbreak unfolded in the early 2000s — and how researchers sought to combat it. (Aired June 2003)

This journalism is made possible by viewers like you. Donate to FRONTLINE now: https://bit.ly/47DFzCb 

And support your local PBS station here: https://www.pbs.org/donate 

The COVID-19 pandemic wasn’t the first time the world experienced an outbreak of a never-before-seen type of coronavirus. In the FRONTLINE/World short documentary “Hong Kong: Chasing the Virus,” which aired in June 2003, reporter and producer Renata Simone went inside an earlier outbreak of a coronavirus that also originated in mainland China: SARS. It spread to the rest of the world after a man from China’s Guangdong province attended a wedding in Hong Kong and unknowingly infected nine other guests at the hotel where he was staying.

As the outbreak unfolded, Simone traveled to Hong Kong. Usually a bustling hub of commerce, the port city had been brought to a virtual standstill. Adding to the fear gripping Hong Kong: There was no cure or proven treatment for SARS.

As the sense of urgency mounted, Simone filmed with an international group of researchers who were teaming up at the University of Hong Kong to try to combat SARS, following their efforts to find a cure. The team included Dr. David Ho, a world-renowned AIDS researcher based at Columbia University in New York who hoped his expertise would be transferable.

By the time the SARS epidemic ultimately wound down that same year, contained through public health measures like testing, quarantine and isolation, close to 800 people had died.

Raney Aronson-Rath. The founder and executive producer of FRONTLINE was David Fanning.

items.title: Kyrgyzstan - The erosion of democracy | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Kyrgyzstan is eroding democratic freedoms, while moving closer to Russia politically. With a feeling of dread, Jama Bekten is organizing what may be the last women's protest to defend their rights.

After the collapse of the Soviet Union, Kyrgyzstan was long considered a democratic outlier in Central Asia. Free elections, a vibrant civil society and independent media set the country apart from its authoritarian neighbors. But since President Sadyr Japarov came to power in 2021, press freedom and political opposition have been increasingly restricted. Critics are being prosecuted, independent media outlets are under pressure and civil society groups are being squeezed by new laws.

At the same time, Kyrgyzstan is experiencing an economic boom. The government touts the country's strong growth and a doubling of the gross domestic product. But part of this boom is linked to shifting flows of trade since Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Russia continues to expand its influence in Kyrgyzstan — including through the Kremlin-aligned Evrazia, also known as the Eurasia Organization, educational projects and the broadcaster Nomad TV. This documentary follows activists, journalists and scholars to show how Kyrgyzstan is evolving from an "island of democracy" into an increasingly authoritarian state.

ABSTRACT
Programming languages are a halfway house between the metal and the mind, a bridge between the world of circuits and the world of applications, the engineered and the social. Programming languages are the medium through which developers codify systems and fragments. In each programming language is embedded a philosophy (or many) of how to think about code, how to organise thoughts, how to design. Programming languages also define skillsets, ecosystems, jobs, loyalties and communities.

When we think of software and technology we often think in terms of progress and rapid change. Programming languages, however, typically move at a far slower pace. Mainstream languages are still embracing ideas that are decades old. Constructs that developers welcome as new to their language of choice are often older than the developers themselves.
And over all this hangs the question, what of the future?
How will current trends, from FOSS to LLMs, shape programming languages and their use?

In this talk, we will take a tour of the past, present and future of programming languages. [...]

items.title: We Need To Talk About Leopold
items.author: Patrick Boyle
items.content:
<article>Taking care of your health just got easier, thanks to my sponsor Zocdoc! Start here at: https://zocdoc.com/patrickboyle

Last week, 24-year-old Leopold Aschenbrenner — former FTX staffer, ex-OpenAI researcher, and author of the viral 165-page essay "Situational Awareness" — managed to lose roughly two-thirds of his $45 billion hedge fund in a matter of weeks. The margin calls arrived during his wedding weekend.

In this video I break down how a trader with no professional experience raised billions from Silicon Valley, why his AI "hedge" wasn't a hedge at all, and how leverage plus a concentrated bet on artificial intelligence stocks turned a great-looking expected return into a catastrophic outcome. Along the way we look at the cultural gap between Silicon Valley and Wall Street, why Ken Griffin's Citadel ended up buying the collapsing portfolio in an overnight fire sale, and the maths of volatility drag — the reason a high expected return can still drag an investor's typical outcome straight into the ground.

It's a story about leverage, risk management, expected versus median returns, and what happens when you go "full Kelly." Featuring reporting from the Wall Street Journal, The New York Times, Bloomberg, and the Financial Times, plus Victor Haghani's lessons from The Missing Billionaires.

items.content:
<article>Mount Kologet, Goldsboro, Palomares, Thule… Four nuclear accidents, four stains on the history of the Cold War. Four names that are now forgotten. These events lay undiscovered for years having been classified as official secrets. Now published, the files show how the relentless standoff between the two superpowers spiralled out of control and led us to the brink of obliteration. 

 Along with contemporary protagonists, historians, geopolitical specialists and atomic experts, this two-episode documentary takes us first to the Uniteted States, then on European soil, to reveal what we avoided by a whisker during a period that is not really all that far in the past. Returning to this subject casts fresh light on the perils to which the public was exposed at a time of extreme tension, especially as recent historiography will allow us to revisit many shadowy corners of the past, throwing up some completely unexpected answers.

items.title: The Shuttle Disaster That Almost Grounded NASA's Dreams | Full Episode 1 | Once Upon a Time in Space
items.author: PBS
items.content:
<article>Watch more from this series: https://to.pbs.org/4eO25vC
At the height of the Cold War, the Soviet Union dominates the space race with a series of firsts, until the U.S. lands the first men on the moon in 1969. With the dawn of the Space Shuttle in 1976, the U.S. gains further ground on its rivals. In 1978, Ron McNair, Anna Fisher and Mike Mullane are among the group selected by NASA to fly aboard the Shuttle after the agency encouraged aspiring astronauts of all genders and racial backgrounds to apply. 
 
Growing up under segregation in South Carolina, McNair had few role models for a life in space beyond Lieutenant Uhura of Star Trek. Vietnam veteran Mullane arrives at NASA skeptical that women or civilians could possess “the right stuff.” Emergency physician Fisher is thrust into the spotlight as the first mother in space. Her decision to leave her one-year-old daughter to fly into space intensifies the scrutiny.
 
As pressure mounts on the Shuttle program to meet military and commercial demands, disaster strikes in 1986 when Challenger explodes during launch, killing all seven astronauts. While the remaining U.S. shuttle fleet is grounded, the Soviet Union successfully launches Mir, the most sophisticated space station ever seen, and edges ahead in the space race.

items.title: Alice Roberts On The Origins of Christianity
items.author: History Hit
items.content:
<article>Dan is joined by author, broadcaster and historian Professor Alice Roberts to examine how Christianity out-organised and outlasted the Roman Empire.

Around 50 CE, a small group of travellers began to preach that a Jewish man, crucified by the Romans, had risen from the dead. Teaching love, forgiveness and eternal life, this new faith quickly gained followers. By the early fourth century, it was thriving, and over the next hundred years, it exploded, spreading across the entire Roman Empire before becoming its official religion. What enabled it to take such a strong hold so quickly and so steadfastly?

ABSTRACT
How do you evolve a framework over nearly two decades without losing the trust of millions of developers? In this talk, I will reflect on 19 years of working on Spring, the Java application framework—from the early days of XML configuration, through the rise of annotations, to the advent of functional programming.

I will share the lessons that come not just from designing APIs and writing code, but from practicing open source stewardship over time. That includes how to innovate under constraints, how to evolve APIs responsibly, how to serve a growing community, and why empathy and restraint are essentials skills when it comes to maintaining open source.

This talk is for anyone willing to learn from my past mistakes, so they can make entirely new ones. [...]

items.title: The Strange Story of America’s First “Alien Abduction”
items.author: Weird History
items.content:
<article>During a late-night drive through rural New Hampshire in 1961, Barney and Betty Hill reported a terrifying encounter with a UFO that would change their lives forever. Since then, their story remains one of the most famous and controversial alien abduction cases in history. From unexplained missing time and hypnotic regression to eerie eyewitness testimony, the Hills' account helped shape modern beliefs about extraterrestrials, UFO sightings, and even the mysteries surrounding Area 51. But were they telling the truth, or did something else happen that night?

In this episode of Weird History Presents: Graveyard Shift, we explore the shocking details behind America's first widely publicized alien abduction case, the evidence that still fuels debate decades later, and why the Barney and Betty Hill story continues to captivate believers and skeptics alike.

Do you think it's possible that the Hills were really abducted by aliens? Let us know in the comments!

items.title: How a Mexican Migrant Farmer’s Journey to the U.S. Turned Fatal (full documentary) | FRONTLINE/World
items.author: FRONTLINE PBS | Official
items.content:
<article>The tragic story of a migrant farmer’s journey to the U.S. in the scorching heat. (Aired June 2004)

This journalism is made possible by viewers like you. Donate to FRONTLINE now: https://bit.ly/47DFzCb 

And support your local PBS station here: https://www.pbs.org/donate 

In “Mexico: A Death in the Desert,” which aired in June 2004, correspondent Claudine LoMonaco documented the story of one migrant worker’s life and death. 

Like many men from Oaxaca, Mexico, Matias Juan Garcia Zavaleta crossed the U.S.-Mexico border regularly each spring to work in California during harvest time and returned in the fall. He used his earnings to build a home and take care of his family. After years of annual crossings, Garcia had had enough of leaving his family, so he planted his own chili pepper crop. But when an early frost destroyed his plants, he was left with no choice but to cross again in the spring of 2003, but this time the crossing turned fatal. 

This FRONTLINE/World short documentary traced Garcia’s journey and the impact of his death on his family. 

“Mexico: A Death in the Desert” was reported and produced by Mary Spicuzza and Claudine LoMonaco. It was produced in association with UC Berkeley Graduate School of Journalism. The founder and executive producer of FRONTLINE was David Fanning. 

We are making episodes from FRONTLINE/World’s archive newly available here on YouTube and on pbs.org as part of an effort to make our past reporting widely accessible.

Originally developed by FRONTLINE producers in conjunction with public television stations KQED San Francisco and WGBH Boston, FRONTLINE/World launched in 2002 as a national public TV series that turned its lens on the global community, covering countries and cultures rarely seen on American television. The series completed its final broadcast season in 2010.

<article>This presentation was recorded at YOW! Australia 2025. #GOTOcon #YOW

Amy Kapernick - Front End Engineer at AmysKapers.dev @amykapernick9407 

RESOURCES

ABSTRACT
While testing is important, we’d much prefer if we didn’t have to think about it, if it just happened like magic.

We know we have to write tests to make sure the buttons can be clicked, the data can be received and the page continues to look the way it should, but once the tests are written, are they actually being run?

We’ve been integrating our end to end tests to ensure they run on every commit or every pull request, but front end tests require a live version of our website to run tests, you can read CSS code in a pull request but that doesn’t tell you if it’s affecting the website the way you intended it to. Thankfully GitHub Actions makes it easy to fix this, to get a live version of our website and run our front end tests against it before the code gets merged and deployed.

Together we’ll build out an action workflow (that can be integrated with your existing end to end tests if you’ve got them), write some front end tests and put together a bulletproof continuous deployment pipeline. [...]

items.title: Why Wall Street is Ignoring Big Tech's Debt
items.author: Patrick Boyle
items.content:
<article>Start your own store with #printify: https://try.printify.com/72vgyfrvedkq
The first 100 people who use the code PATRICK will get 15% off their first order!

Nikkei Asia recently reported that the five biggest US tech companies are carrying an estimated $1.65 trillion in "hidden," off-balance-sheet debt — and a lot of commentators have reached for the word "Enron" to describe the issue. In this video I look at whether that comparison holds up. It doesn't: unlike Enron, this debt isn't concealed through fraud — it's disclosed in the footnotes, it breaks no accounting rules, and much of what is going on is perfectly ordinary. But that raises a more interesting question than "will they get caught." If the aggressive stuff — the adjusted earnings, the leases, the stock-based compensation added back — is all sitting there in plain sight, does dressing up the numbers actually fool anyone? Drawing on the work of Aswath Damodaran, Richard Sloan, Robert Bloomfield and others, I dig into what the research says about whether markets reward clean accounting or aggressive accounting, why the debt isn't hidden so much as filed somewhere too tedious for most people to read — and why the real risk in the AI boom probably isn't the borrowing at all, but the enormous revenue it's all assuming will show up.

items.title: How Rats Helped Save Human Lives | Tanzania: Hero Rats (full documentary) | FRONTLINE/World
items.author: FRONTLINE PBS | Official
items.content:
<article>Go inside an effort to train giant rats to sniff out deadly unexploded land mines — and save lives. (Aired 2007)

This journalism is made possible by viewers like you. Donate to FRONTLINE now: https://bit.ly/47DFzCb 

And support your local PBS station here: https://www.pbs.org/donate

Bart Weetjens founded a unique lab in Tanzania dedicated to training rats to sniff out deadly unexploded land mines — the legacy of countless bloody conflicts. Although dogs had traditionally been used to help humans detect mines, Weetjens, who had long felt a special bond with rodents, realized that African giant pouched rats were lighter, cheaper to care for, and less susceptible to tropical disease.

In “Hero Rats,” FRONTLINE/World reporter Alexis Bloom accompanied Weetjens to neighboring Mozambique to watch his organization’s trained rodents in action. She also visited a school there that was cleared of landmines with the help of the rats, allowing the children to resume their education and play without fear of stepping on a mine. The rats save human lives, Weetjens said, “and, yes, they are heroes, actually.”

“Tanzania: Hero Rats” was produced by Cassandra Herrman. It was reported by Alexis Bloom. For FRONTLINE/World, the coordinating producer was David Ritsher and the senior producer was Ken Dornstein. The founder and executive producer of FRONTLINE was David Fanning.

items.title: Where is Venezuela’s oil money?
items.author: Patrick Boyle
items.content:
<article>If you’re looking to upgrade your business wardrobe, I can recommend giving Tailor Store a try. Their shirts are made to your measurements, so you can create something that fits both your body and your personal style. My viewers receive 25% off their first order through my link: https://www.tailorstore.com/patrickboyle

When the United States took control of Venezuela's oil exports in early 2026, it collected an estimated $13 billion in crude sales — but the official ledger in Caracas records almost none of it, and six months on there is still no public accounting of where the money went. In this video we look at what happened to Venezuela's sovereign wealth: the missing oil revenues now sitting in an offshore account in Qatar, the four billion dollars of Venezuelan gold frozen in the vaults of the Bank of England that no one can legally claim, and the court-ordered auction that handed Citgo's parent company to an affiliate of Paul Singer's Elliott Management for nearly $6 billion. Along the way we explain the legal machinery that makes all of this possible — the alter ego doctrine, sovereign immunity and the Bancec ruling, the Terrorism Risk Insurance Act, and the "one voice" principle in English law — and the broader lesson for anyone trying to understand sovereign assets: a nation's wealth held abroad is only yours for as long as someone else's courts, banks and vaults agree that it is. We also cover the aftermath of the June earthquakes, the international relief effort, and why the question of who legitimately governs Venezuela sits at the centre of every one of these disputes.
